children: On Tuesday, Elon Musk revealed that Tesla
and SpaceX
have established committees to explore a merger combination.
We asked Seeking Alpha analysts
, and
how much they thought Tesla could be worth in a merger deal.

Danil Sereda: There are actually many moving parts here. Usually, boards establish independent special committees to determine the price. Musk said the companies had already formed special committees, so I'd expect the merger to close within the next year or two.
We know that Tesla
produces positive operating cash flow (>$18B on a TTM basis, per Seeking Alpha). It also holds ~$43.5B in liquid cash and investments, whereas SpaceX

burned over $42B in CapEx on a TTM basis (mainly on its orbital infrastructure and AI-related stuff). So I agree with some analysts who say that Tesla shareholders might be willing to take >50% control of the combined entity (that's an assumption from Morningstar).

I'll take 50% here to account for SPCX's structurally higher valuation at the start because it has more growth pillars. At 50% of the combined market cap right now (~$3.5T), I'm getting to $1.75T for TSLA, which has ~3.95B diluted shares outstanding. This gives me a fair value per share of $443, which is around 20% above today's price (I'm comparing to the pre-market price of ~$368/share on Thursday, Oct. 22). Of course, the proportion might be above 50% for Tesla, and in that case, the premium will be higher.
(Danil Sereda leads the SA investing group Beyond the Wall Investing.)
Victor Dergunov: I think SpaceX
would pay $420 to $500 per share at the very least for Tesla

, and that is if the deal went through in the very near term. However, the high-interest environment may push the deal to mid-2027 or so. It's possible the markets may be more optimistic because of easier Fed policy by then, and I'd prefer $550 or more for my shares, as it is my portfolio's most considerable position. I also want to increase my position on any pullbacks in Tesla's stock in future weeks and months.
Carla Magliocco: In an article I wrote in May about Tesla
and its vertical integration, a user asked me how the IPO of SpaceX
, which took place the following month, would affect Tesla
. There were plenty of doubts about it, and it was believed that Tesla investors would sell their shares and rush toward SpaceX
. But none of that happened.

So, at that moment, my answer was yes, I'd love a merger because it would unite all the potential of the physical AI that Tesla was already developing. Since at least 2023, Musk has said he wanted to base his corporate ecosystem on AI. And I believe that makes sense.
In the preview of Q3 that I wrote about Tesla

earlier this week, I explained that the FSD model is precisely that: a platform that builds an empire of physical AI. In the preview, I estimated 1.62M active subscribers, but I fell short: there were 1.74M, representing 67% year-over-year growth.
But now, such a merger would benefit even more the sentiment of Tesla investors, and as I own shares of Tesla
and not SpaceX

, this really excites me. But it's more about a mutual benefit. SpaceX just showed in its Q3 results that its Super Intelligence segment is not only growing more than expected but is also reaching higher profitability.
Meanwhile, Tesla

still doesn't show strong profitability, and that's why it needs more investment to accelerate the production of Robotaxis and Optimus and reach a more advanced FSD system without supervision. At the same time, Tesla would give SpaceX
what SpaceX doesn't have: monetization of its physical AI. Therefore, I believe that any news about a merger would make Tesla rise, although the final result will depend on the terms.
